newsitem.title: USA: Retail sales fell in April in another sign of slowdown.
newsitem.headline: Retail sales fell in April in another sign of slowdown.

text.p: Retail sales fell at the steepest rate in 10 months in April, the government said Tuesday, as consumers spent less on cars, clothes and other items in what could be a key sign of slower economic growth.

Total retail sales fell 0.3 percent to a seasonally adjusted $212.2 billion -- the biggest decline since a 0.5 percent drop last June -- after sales were unchanged in March, the Commerce Department said. The department had previously estimated sales rose 0.1 percent in March.

Cold, rainy weather in many regions helped fuel the decline. Economists said the signs of slower demand were sure to be noted by Federal Reserve policy-makers who meet next Tuesday to weigh whether to raise interest rates again.

"These data indicate that consumer spending came to a screeching halt in March, relative to the very strong consumer spending which took place in December, January and February," said economist Marilyn Schaja of Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp. in New York.

Schaja said she now felt the odds of another rate increase by the Fed on May 20 were less than even. The central bank raised short-term rates a quarter point on March 25, the first increase in more than two years, in a bid to slow demand and ward off inflation.
The broad-based April sales decline came after other reports have pointed to slower spending by consumers, whose purchases of goods and services fuel two-thirds of the economy.
Automakers said last week that sales of U.S.-built cars and light trucks fell in April to the slowest rate in 18 months. Retailers also reported weak sales compared to March.

In its report, the Commerce Department said car dealers said sales fell 0.9 percent in April, the steepest drop since November, after a 0.3 percent March decline. New cars account for a quarter of retail sales.
Even excluding autos, retail sales still fell 0.1 percent last month after a 0.1 percent rise in March.
Sales at retail stores fell 0.9 percent after a 0.1 percent decline in March. Clothing store sales slipped 0.6 percent after falling 1 percent in March.
Not all analysts were convinced a major slowdown was under way.

"We had an extraordinary first quarter for retail sales, ... so April's decline represents perhaps more of a correction than a fundamental deterioration for household expenditures," said John Lonski, senior economist at Moody's Investors Service in New York.
Consumer spending is so important to the economy that Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan mentioned it last week, noting he was looking for firm evidence that it was easing.

"Should the expected slowing in the growth of demand fail to materialize, we would need to address any emerging pressures in product and credit markets," the Fed chief said in a speech in New York on Thursday. Economists said Greenspan meant he was ready to raise rates again, but whether the Fed would do so remained an open question.
The economy grew at a 5.6 percent rate in the first quarter, the strongest in more than nine years, and the Fed is watching closely for signs that inflation may be accelerating.
Sales of building materals were flat in April after rising 1 percent in March. Analysts had said cold weather and flooding in some regions had probably slowed construction.
Gasoline station sales dropped 0.1 percent in April after a 0.5 percent decline in March.

Economist Rosalind Wells of the Washington-based National Retail Federation, said that both March and April retail sales were "less than robust" but added that strong job creation and income growth should boost sales later in the year.
